title: Contractions of *be*
lede: *I'm*, *you're*, *it's*, *that's* — the commonest contractions in the language, and the ones that hide an apostrophe trap.
intro: Every one of these joins a subject to a form of *be*. Two of them are the most-corrected spellings in English: ***it's*** is *it is* or *it has* and never a possessive (*its* is the possessive), and ***you're*** is *you are*, not *your*. The last, *let's*, is the odd one — the *'s* there is *us*, not *is*.

title: Contractions of *have* and *had*
lede: *I've*, *could've*, *I'd* — including the *'d* that is sometimes *had* and sometimes *would*.
intro: *'ve* is always *have*. *'d* is the ambiguous one: *I'd gone* is *had*, *I'd go* is *would*, and only the verb that follows tells you which. The *-'ve* of *could've* sounds exactly like *of*, which is why *could of* is the most common spelling error in written American English — it is never correct.

title: Contractions of *will*
lede: *I'll*, *it'll*, *there'll* — the future contracted onto the subject.
intro: *'ll* is *will* after any subject. In fast speech it almost disappears — *I'll* is often just a lengthened *I* with an /l/ — which is why learners frequently do not hear the future at all. Note that *he'll* and *heal*, *we'll* and *wheel*, *I'll* and *aisle* are near or exact homophones.

title: Negative contractions
lede: *don't*, *isn't*, *won't*, *can't* — *not* joined to the verb, and the forms English does not have.
intro: These join *not* to an auxiliary or modal. Three are irregular in sound or spelling: ***won't*** (not *willn't*), ***can't***, and ***shan't***, which has all but vanished from American English. The question form is where learners slip: the contraction inverts as one word — *Isn't he coming?* — and the first-person question is ***aren't I?***, since English has no *amn't*.

title: Spoken reductions and informal forms
lede: *gonna*, *wanna*, *y'all*, *'em* — what English actually sounds like, and where you may write it.
intro: These are not contractions of the neat kind: they are spellings of ordinary fast speech. Every American says *gonna* and *wanna*; almost nobody writes them outside dialogue and text messages. They are worth knowing because you will hear them constantly and because a few have grammar of their own — *gonna* only works for the future, never for movement: *I'm gonna leave* is fine, but *I'm gonna the store* is not English.
